claim: The protein dynamical transition occurs at approximately 200 K.
source: The protein dynamical transition at ~200 K, where the biomolecule transforms from a harmonic, non-functional form to an anharmonic, functional state, has been thought to be slaved to the thermal activation of dynamics in its surface hydration water.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known phenomenon being investigated.

claim: At the dynamical transition, the biomolecule transforms from a harmonic, non-functional form to an anharmonic, functional state.
source: The protein dynamical transition at ~200 K, where the biomolecule transforms from a harmonic, non-functional form to an anharmonic, functional state, has been thought to be slaved to the thermal activation of dynamics in its surface hydration water.
evidence: This characterization of the transition is stated in the abstract.

claim: The onset of anharmonicity in protein and hydration water around 200 K is decoupled.
source: Here, by selectively probing the dynamics of protein and hydration water using elastic neutron scattering and isotopic labeling, we found that the onset of anharmonicity in the two components around 200 K is decoupled.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from elastic neutron scattering.

claim: The onset of anharmonicity in protein is an intrinsic transition whose characteristic temperature is independent of the instrumental resolution time.
source: The one in protein is an intrinsic transition, whose characteristic temperature is independent of the instrumental resolution time, but varies with the biomolecular structure and the amount of hydration, while the one of water is merely a resolution effect.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by measurements at different instrumental resolutions shown in Figure 1.

claim: The onset temperature of the protein dynamical transition varies with the biomolecular structure.
source: The one in protein is an intrinsic transition, whose characteristic temperature is independent of the instrumental resolution time, but varies with the biomolecular structure and the amount of hydration, while the one of water is merely a resolution effect.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by comparing different proteins (LYS, MYO, CYP) in Figure 1.

claim: The onset temperature of the protein dynamical transition varies with the amount of hydration.
source: The one in protein is an intrinsic transition, whose characteristic temperature is independent of the instrumental resolution time, but varies with the biomolecular structure and the amount of hydration, while the one of water is merely a resolution effect.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by measurements at different hydration levels shown in Figure 2.

claim: The onset of anharmonicity in hydration water is merely a resolution effect.
source: The one in protein is an intrinsic transition, whose characteristic temperature is independent of the instrumental resolution time, but varies with the biomolecular structure and the amount of hydration, while the one of water is merely a resolution effect.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by measurements showing resolution-dependent onset temperatures for water in Figure 3.

claim: Internal dynamics of a protein is crucial for its functions, including allosteric conformational changes.
source: It is well established that the internal dynamics of a protein is crucial for its functions, including allosteric conformational changes (Martin, 2001), ligand binding (Balog et al., 2004) and enzymatic reactions (Hay and Scrutton, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Internal dynamics of a protein is crucial for ligand binding.
source: It is well established that the internal dynamics of a protein is crucial for its functions, including allosteric conformational changes (Martin, 2001), ligand binding (Balog et al., 2004) and enzymatic reactions (Hay and Scrutton, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Internal dynamics of a protein is crucial for enzymatic reactions.
source: It is well established that the internal dynamics of a protein is crucial for its functions, including allosteric conformational changes (Martin, 2001), ligand binding (Balog et al., 2004) and enzymatic reactions (Hay and Scrutton, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Hydrated proteins exhibit a dynamical transition around 200 K where the slope of the temperature dependence of atomic displacements changes significantly.
source: In particular, hydrated proteins exhibit a dynamical transition around 200 K, across which the slope of the temperature dependence of the atomic displacements changes significantly and the biomolecule transforms from a rigid, harmonic state, to a flexible, anharmonic form (Rupley and Careri, 1991; Vitkup et al., 2000; Rasmussen et al., 1992; Wood et al., 2008; Roh et al., 2005; Zaccai, 2000; Doster et al., 1989; Hong et al., 2013; Schiró et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The dynamical transition has been linked to the thermal onset of function in myoglobin.
source: Although exceptions have been reported (Daniel et al., 1998), the dynamical transition has been linked to the thermal onset of function in a number of proteins, for example, myoglobin (MYO; Austin et al., 1975), ribonuclease (Rasmussen et al., 1992), elastase (Ding et al., 1994), and bacteriorhodopsin (Ferrand et al., 1993), all of which become inactive below the dynamical transition temperature.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The dynamical transition has been linked to the thermal onset of function in ribonuclease.
source: Although exceptions have been reported (Daniel et al., 1998), the dynamical transition has been linked to the thermal onset of function in a number of proteins, for example, myoglobin (MYO; Austin et al., 1975), ribonuclease (Rasmussen et al., 1992), elastase (Ding et al., 1994), and bacteriorhodopsin (Ferrand et al., 1993), all of which become inactive below the dynamical transition temperature.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The dynamical transition has been linked to the thermal onset of function in elastase.
source: Although exceptions have been reported (Daniel et al., 1998), the dynamical transition has been linked to the thermal onset of function in a number of proteins, for example, myoglobin (MYO; Austin et al., 1975), ribonuclease (Rasmussen et al., 1992), elastase (Ding et al., 1994), and bacteriorhodopsin (Ferrand et al., 1993), all of which become inactive below the dynamical transition temperature.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The dynamical transition has been linked to the thermal onset of function in bacteriorhodopsin.
source: Although exceptions have been reported (Daniel et al., 1998), the dynamical transition has been linked to the thermal onset of function in a number of proteins, for example, myoglobin (MYO; Austin et al., 1975), ribonuclease (Rasmussen et al., 1992), elastase (Ding et al., 1994), and bacteriorhodopsin (Ferrand et al., 1993), all of which become inactive below the dynamical transition temperature.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Myoglobin, ribonuclease, elastase, and bacteriorhodopsin become inactive below the dynamical transition temperature.
source: Although exceptions have been reported (Daniel et al., 1998), the dynamical transition has been linked to the thermal onset of function in a number of proteins, for example, myoglobin (MYO; Austin et al., 1975), ribonuclease (Rasmussen et al., 1992), elastase (Ding et al., 1994), and bacteriorhodopsin (Ferrand et al., 1993), all of which become inactive below the dynamical transition temperature.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: One theory suggests the protein dynamical transition is due to the behavior of water in the hydration shell, transitioning from rigid to fluid at certain temperatures.
source: One theory suggests it is due to the behavior of water in the hydration shell, transitioning from rigid to fluid at certain temperatures, thus influencing protein flexibility (Wood et al., 2008; Schiró et al., 2012; Fenimore et al., 2002; Frauenfelder et al., 2009; Qin et al., 2016; Lewandowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an existing theory with supporting citations.

claim: Another theory considers the dynamical transition as an inherent property of the protein, where thermal energy allows the protein to access a wider range of conformations.
source: Another theory considers the transition as an inherent property of the protein, where thermal energy allows the protein to access a wider range of conformations (Nickels et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an alternative theory with a supporting citation.

claim: A prevailing scenario is that the internal dynamics of the protein is slaved to the motion of the surrounding hydration water.
source: A prevailing scenario is that the internal dynamics of the protein is slaved to the motion of the surrounding hydration water (Wood et al., 2008; Schiró et al., 2012; Fenimore et al., 2002; Frauenfelder et al., 2009; Qin et al., 2016; Lewandowski et al., 2015), and thus the protein dynamical transition results from the changes in the dynamics of the hydration water with temperature (Vitkup et al., 2000; Wood et al., 2008; Schiró et al., 2012; Frauenfelder et al., 2009; Tournier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a prevailing scenario with supporting citations.

claim: The presence of the protein dynamical transition requires a minimum amount of hydration water, approximately 0.2 g water/g protein.
source: This scenario is indirectly supported by the experimental finding that the presence of the protein dynamical transition requires a minimum amount of hydration water, ~0.2 g water/g protein (Rupley and Careri, 1991; Roh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with supporting citations.

claim: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations suggest that the activation of translational motions of surface water molecules around 200 K leads to the dynamical transition in the underlying protein.
source: Further support comes from the results of all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, suggesting that it is the activation of the translational motions of surface water molecules around 200 K that leads to the dynamical transition in the underlying protein (Vitkup et al., 2000; Wood et al., 2008; Tournier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from simulations with supporting citations.

claim: Neutrons are highly sensitive to hydrogen atoms as their incoherent scattering cross section is an order of magnitude higher than the incoherent and coherent scattering cross sections of other elements.
source: Neutrons are highly sensitive to hydrogen atoms as their incoherent scattering cross section is an order of magnitude higher than the incoherent and coherent scattering cross sections of other elements (Liu et al., 2017; Gaspar et al., 2010; Hong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a known property of neutron scattering with supporting citations.

claim: Neutron signals collected on an ordinary protein powder hydrated in D2O reflect the dynamics of the protein.
source: Thus, neutron signals collected on an ordinary protein powder hydrated in D2O reflect the dynamics of the protein while signals from the perdeuterated sample in H2O inform about the motion of water.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the differential scattering properties of hydrogen and deuterium.

claim: Neutron signals from perdeuterated protein samples in H2O inform about the motion of water.
source: Thus, neutron signals collected on an ordinary protein powder hydrated in D2O reflect the dynamics of the protein while signals from the perdeuterated sample in H2O inform about the motion of water.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the differential scattering properties of hydrogen and deuterium.

claim: Measurements on perdeuterated maltose-binding protein hydrated in H2O revealed a harmonic-to-anharmonic transition for hydration water taking place at the same temperature as that of the underlying protein.
source: Measurements performed on perdeuterated maltose-binding protein hydrated in H2O revealed a harmonic-to-anharmonic transition for hydration water taking place at the same temperature as that of the underlying protein (Wood et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a previous experimental result with a supporting citation.

claim: An experiment on perdeuterated green fluorescence protein showed that the anharmonic onset in hydration water occurs at a lower temperature than that of the protein.
source: In contrast, a similar experiment on perdeuterated green fluorescence protein showed that the anharmonic onset in hydration water occurs at a lower temperature than that of the protein (Nickels et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a previous experimental result with a supporting citation.

claim: Measurements on lysozyme hydrated in both D2O and H2O found that the transition temperature of protein and water coincided when examining their atomic displacements at 1 ns.
source: More recent measurements on lysozyme (LYS) hydrated in both D2O and H2O found that the transition temperature of protein and water coincided when examining their atomic displacements at 1 ns, but took place at different temperatures when changing the explored time scale to 3 ns (Benedetto, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a previous experimental result with a supporting citation.

claim: Measurements on lysozyme hydrated in both D2O and H2O found that the transition temperatures of protein and water took place at different temperatures when changing the explored time scale to 3 ns.
source: More recent measurements on lysozyme (LYS) hydrated in both D2O and H2O found that the transition temperature of protein and water coincided when examining their atomic displacements at 1 ns, but took place at different temperatures when changing the explored time scale to 3 ns (Benedetto, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a previous experimental result with a supporting citation.

claim: The onset temperature (Ton) of the protein dynamical transition for LYS is 213 K.
source: Two important conclusions can be drawn from Figure 1 (Ton is summarized in Table 5). (1) Ton is distinct for each protein, LYS (213 K), MYO (198 K), and CYP (228 K), and (2) it is independent of the time scale explored even though the resolutions of the neutron spectrometers differ by orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Table 5.

source: Two important conclusions can be drawn from Figure 1 (Ton is summarized in Table 5). (1) Ton is distinct for each protein, LYS (213 K), MYO (198 K), and CYP (228 K), and (2) it is independent of the time scale explored even though the resolutions of the neutron spectrometers differ by orders of magnitude.

evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Table 5.

source: Two important conclusions can be drawn from Figure 1 (Ton is summarized in Table 5). (1) Ton is distinct for each protein, LYS (213 K), MYO (198 K), and CYP (228 K), and (2) it is independent of the time scale explored even though the resolutions of the neutron spectrometers differ by orders of magnitude.

claim: Ton of H-CYP increases from 228 to 248 K when reducing hydration level from 0.4 to 0.2.
source: Evidently Ton of the protein increases from 228 to 248 K when reducing h from 0.4 to 0.2 (Figure 2a) by using the neutron instrument with Δt = 1 ns.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Ton of LYS changes systematically from 195 to 225 K when decreasing hydration level from 0.45 to 0.18.
source: It can be found that Ton of LYS changes systematically from 195 to 225 K, when decreasing h from 0.45 to 0.18.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by replotted data from Roh et al., 2006 shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The extent of hydration does not alter the protein secondary structure content and overall packing of CYP.
source: We also studied the secondary structure content and tertiary structure of CYP protein at different hydration levels (h = 0.2 and 0.4) through molecular dynamics simulation. As shown in Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, the extent of hydration does not alter the protein secondary structure content and overall packing.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by molecular dynamics simulation results shown in Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Water molecules have more influence on protein dynamics than on protein structure.
source: Thus, this result suggests that water molecules have more influence on protein dynamics than on protein structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that hydration affects dynamics but not structure.

claim: H-CYP at h = 0.2 and h = 0.4 exhibit a step-like transition in the heat flow at 245 and 225 K, respectively.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2b, H-CYP at h = 0.2 and h = 0.4 exhibit a step-like transition in the heat flow at 245 and 225 K, respectively, while no such transition is observed in dry H-CYP.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by DSC data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: No step-like transition in heat flow is observed in dry H-CYP.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2b, H-CYP at h = 0.2 and h = 0.4 exhibit a step-like transition in the heat flow at 245 and 225 K, respectively, while no such transition is observed in dry H-CYP.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by DSC data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Step-like transition in heat flow is normally defined as the glass transition in polymers.
source: Such step-like transition in heat flow is normally defined as the glass transition in polymers (Bassi et al., 2003; Stolwijk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a known definition with supporting citations.

claim: The values of TDSC approximate those of Ton probed by neutrons.
source: When comparing Figure 2b with Figure 2a, one can find that the values of TDSC approximate those of Ton probed by neutrons.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be verified by comparing the data in Figures 2a and 2b.

claim: TDSC of hydrated MYO is 190 K.
source: TDSC of hydrated MYO was reported by literature to be 190 K (Jansson and Swenson, 2010), which is again in good agreement with the value of Ton in Figure 1.

claim: The onset of anharmonicity around 200 K in proteins measured by neutron scattering results from the freezing of the structural relaxation of the biomolecule beyond the equilibrium when cooling the system below TDSC, similar to the glass transition in polymers.
source: Therefore, we can conclude that the onset of anharmonicity around 200 K in proteins measured by neutron scattering as shown in Figure 1 results from the freezing of the structural relaxation of the biomolecule beyond the equilibrium when cooling the system below TDSC, similar to the glass transition in polymers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of neutron scattering and DSC data.

claim: Freezing of the structural relaxation beyond the equilibrium time will turn the system into a frozen solid form, which can significantly suppress the fast dynamics measured by neutron.
source: However, 'freezing' of the structural relaxation beyond the equilibrium time (~100–1000 s), that is, the measurement time of neutron experiments at each temperature, will turn the system into a 'frozen' solid form, which can significantly suppress the fast dynamics measured by neutron and cause the transition probed (Ngai, 2004; Frick and Richter, 1995; Frick et al., 1995; Ngai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation with supporting citations.

claim: Water can be considered as lubricant or plasticizer which facilitates the motion of the biomolecule.
source: Moreover, water can be considered here as lubricant or plasticizer which facilitates the motion of the biomolecule (Hong et al., 2012; Roh et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Adding water as plasticizer significantly reduces the glass transition temperature of polymers.
source: As widely observed in polymeric systems (Verhoeven et al., 1989; Zhang et al., 1999; Cerveny et al., 2005), adding water as plasticizer will significantly reduce the glass transition temperature of the polymers.
evidence: This is stated as a known phenomenon in polymer science with supporting citations.

claim: Ton of hydration water for GFP and CYP strongly depends on the resolution of the spectrometer, increasing drastically from 200 to 250 K when reducing Δt from 1 ns to 10 ps.
source: Two important observations arise from the data. First, Ton of hydration water for these two proteins strongly depends on the resolution of the spectrometer, increasing drastically from 200 to 250 K when reducing Δt from 1 ns to 10 ps.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The relaxation time of hydration water is 10 ps at 250 K, 40 ps at 234 K, and 1 ns at 200 K.
source: In this case, it means that the relaxation time, τ, of hydration water is 10 ps at 250 K, 40 ps at 234 K, and 1 ns at 200 K.
evidence: This is inferred from the resolution-dependent onset temperatures observed in the neutron scattering data.

claim: The anharmonic onset of the hydration water is not a real physical transition but merely a resolution effect.
source: Our results thus demonstrate that the anharmonic onset of the hydration water is in fact not a real physical transition but merely a resolution effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the resolution-dependent behavior observed in the neutron scattering data.

claim: The anharmonic onset of hydration water occurs as the relaxation time of water crosses the instrument resolution on the pico-to-nanosecond time scales at Ton.
source: It occurs as the relaxation time τ of water, which varies continuously with temperature, happens to cross the instrument resolution, Δt, on the pico-to-nanosecond time scales at Ton.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the resolution effect.

claim: Dielectric measurements showed a smooth temperature dependence of the characteristic relaxation time of hydration water in the range from 170 to 250 K without any sudden changes.
source: Our findings agree with reports from dielectric measurements, the signal of which is highly sensitive to the rotation of hydration water (Pawlus et al., 2008; Khodadadi et al., 2008). They showed a smooth temperature dependence of the characteristic relaxation time in the range from 170 to 250 K without any sudden changes (Pawlus et al., 2008; Khodadadi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The characteristic relaxation time of protein-surface water changes smoothly over temperature without any disruptions around the dynamical transition temperature of the protein.
source: Moreover, our data also agree with Doster et al., 2010, which demonstrated that the characteristic relaxation time of protein-surface water, measured on H2O-hydrated perdeuterated C-phycocyanin by quasi-elastic neutron scattering, changes smoothly over temperature without any disruptions around the dynamical transition temperature of the protein.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The onset temperature of the hydration water is independent of the protein structure when the instrument resolution is fixed.
source: Second, the onset temperature of the hydration water is independent of the protein structure when Δt is fixed, since the values of both GFP and CYP are identical.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ton of hydration water remains constant with hydration level as long as the instrument resolution is fixed.
source: Furthermore, the hydration dependence of the anharmonic onset of the water is presented in Figure 4, which shows that Ton remains constant with h as long as the instrument resolution is fixed.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The anharmonic onsets of protein and surface water around 200 K are clearly decoupled and different in origin.
source: By combining elastic neutron scattering with isotopic labeling, we have been able to probe the dynamics of the protein and surface water separately, as a function of temperature, protein structural composition, hydration level, and time scale. We found that the anharmonic onsets of the two components around 200 K are clearly decoupled and different in origin.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: The protein shows an intrinsic transition whose temperature depends on the structure of the protein and the hydration level, and not on the instrument used to measure it.
source: The protein shows an intrinsic transition, whose temperature depends on the structure of the protein and the hydration level, and not on the instrument used to measure it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing resolution-independent but structure- and hydration-dependent onset temperatures for proteins.

claim: The protein dynamical transition has a thermodynamic signature similar to the glass transition in polymers as confirmed by DSC.
source: It has a thermodynamic signature similar to the glass transition in polymers as confirmed by DSC, and thus can be assigned to the freezing of the structural relaxation of the protein beyond the experimental equilibrium time (100–1000 s).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by DSC measurements.

claim: The temperature at which the onset of anharmonicity happens in the hydration water is given by the instrument resolution, independent of both the biomolecular structure and the level of hydration.
source: In contrast, the temperature at which the onset of anharmonicity happens in the hydration water is given by the instrument resolution, independent of both the biomolecular structure and the level of hydration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing resolution-dependent but structure- and hydration-independent onset temperatures for water.

claim: In some cases, the dynamical transition of a protein can coincide with the anharmonic onset of its surface water if one characterizes the system using a single-neutron instrument with a fixed resolution.
source: Based on our findings, we can infer that, in some cases, the dynamical transition of a protein can coincide with the anharmonic onset of its surface water if one characterizes the system using a single-neutron instrument with a fixed resolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings of the study.

claim: The coincidence between protein dynamical transition and water anharmonic onset will be torn apart if the measurements were conducted using instruments of different resolutions or at different amounts of hydration.
source: But such coincidence will be torn apart if the measurements were conducted by using instruments of different resolutions or at different amounts of hydration, such as in the present work.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the contradictory results in the literature.

claim: The protein dynamical transition is an intrinsic property of the hydrated protein that its structural relaxation is activated upon heating above the onset temperature.
source: The protein dynamical transition has long been thought to connect to the thermal onset of the functionality of the biomolecule. Our experiments suggest that this transition in protein is an intrinsic property of the hydrated protein that its structural relaxation is activated upon heating above the onset temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Unfreezing of the protein structural relaxation might facilitate conformational jumps among different functional states, turning on its functionality.
source: This structural relaxation might be associated with conformational jumps of the biomolecules among different functional states, such as the states with the ligand-binding pocket being opened or closed. Unfreezing of the protein structural relaxation might facilitate these conformational jumps, turning on its functionality.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the functional implications of the structural relaxation.

claim: The denatured form of LYS exhibits a dynamical transition similar to that seen in its folded native form.
source: However, as revealed by Mamontov et al., 2010, the denatured form of LYS also exhibits a dynamical transition, similar to that seen in its folded native form.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The dynamical transition can be found in the mixture of amino acids.
source: Additionally, the dynamical transition also can be found in the mixture of amino acids (Schiró et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The activation of the structural relaxation of the biomolecule above the dynamical transition temperature is a necessary but insufficient condition for the protein to function.
source: Hence, one can argue that the activation of the structural relaxation of the biomolecule above the dynamical transition temperature is a necessary but insufficient condition for the protein to function, as the latter also requires the biomolecule assuming the correctly folded three-dimensional structure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations about denatured proteins and amino acid mixtures.

claim: The protein dynamical transition is a real transition, connecting to unfreezing of the biomolecular structural relaxation, which could be crucial for activating the function.
source: More importantly, we demonstrated that the protein dynamical transition is a real transition, connecting to unfreezing of the biomolecular structural relaxation, which could be crucial for activating the function.
evidence: This is stated as a key conclusion of the study.

claim: Three neutron backscattering spectrometers were used: HFBS at the NIST Center for Neutron Scattering, DNA at the Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility at J-PARC in Japan, and OSIRIS at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Facility, UK.
source: Three neutron backscattering spectrometers were chosen to cover a wide range of time scales; HFBS at the NIST Center for Neutron Scattering, USA, DNA at the Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility at J-PARC in Japan, and OSIRIS at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Facility, UK.

evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The elastic scattering intensity S(q, Δt) is an estimate of the average amplitude of the atomic motions up to Δt.
source: The quantity measured in the neutron experiment is the elastic intensity, that is the intensity of the elastic peak in the dynamic structure factor, S(q, Δt), where q is the scattering wave vector and Δt is the resolution time of the neutron spectrometer. S(q, Δt) is an estimate of the average amplitude of the atomic motions up to Δt (Hong et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: A clear deviation can be seen in the temperature dependence of S(q, Δt) for the hydrated protein from that of the dry powder, which is defined as the onset temperature, Ton, of the protein dynamical transition.
source: A clear deviation can be seen in the temperature dependence of S(q, Δt) for the hydrated protein from that of the dry powder, which is defined as the onset temperature, Ton (Roh et al., 2005; Schiró et al., 2012; Benedetto, 2017; Roh et al., 2006; Schirò et al., 2015), of the protein dynamical transition.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The definition of Ton highlights the effect of hydration on the anharmonic dynamics in proteins while removing the contribution from the local side groups, for example, methyl groups, whose motions are hydration independent.
source: The advantage of such definition is that it highlights the effect of hydration on the anharmonic dynamics in proteins while removing the contribution from the local side groups, for example, methyl groups, whose motions are hydration independent (Hong et al., 2013; Hong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The activation temperature of the rotations of methyl groups varies with the instrument resolution.
source: As shown in Schiró et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2018, the activation temperature of the rotations of methyl group varies with the instrument resolution, which will cloud the present analysis.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The q-range does not alter the Ton of proteins.
source: We further calculated Ton of H-protein in D2O in the q-range from 0.45 to 0.9 and 1.1 to 1.75 Å−1. As shown in Table 3, Table 4, and Table 5, the q-range does not alter the Ton of proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Tables 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The dynamical transition temperature in lipid membranes is higher when the membrane is dry.
source: The dynamical transition temperature in lipid membranes is higher when the membrane is dry (Popova and Hincha, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Ton in both protein and polypeptide is independent of the resolution of the neutron spectrometer if one carefully removes the contributions from methyl rotations and vibrations to <x2(Δt)> measured by elastic neutron scattering.
source: Our results are consistent with Schiró et al., 2012, which demonstrated that Ton in both protein and polypeptide is independent of the resolution of the neutron spectrometer, if one carefully removes the contributions from methyl rotations and vibrations to <x2(Δt)>measured by elastic neutron scattering.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: D2O-hydrated LYS presents an approximately resolution-independent Ton compared to the dry form.
source: Additionally, Benedetto, 2017 showed that, as compared to the dry form, the D2O-hydrated LYS presents an approximately resolution-independent Ton, again in agreement with our findings.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The CHARMM 27 force field was used for CYP in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: The CHARMM 27 force field in the GROMACS package was used for CYP, whereas the TIP4P/Ew model was chosen for water.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The TIP4P/Ew model was chosen for water in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: The CHARMM 27 force field in the GROMACS package was used for CYP, whereas the TIP4P/Ew model was chosen for water.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations were carried out at temperatures ranging from 360 to 100 K with a step of 5 K.
source: The simulations were carried out at a broad range of temperatures from 360 to 100 K, with a step of 5 K.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: A 30-ns NPT simulation is sufficient to equilibrate the CYP system.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3, 30 ns is sufficient to equilibrate the system.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3.
